Strategic Intelligence Briefing

Biomedical Research Landscape
2024–2026

A comprehensive trend analysis of 126,832 biomedical research abstracts indexed in PubMed, examining temporal publication patterns, geographic contributions, dominant research topics, and open-access adoption.

Audience: Research Policy Analysts & Funding Strategists Data Source: PubMed / NCBI · Kaggle Coverage: January 2024 – March 2026 Published: April 2026
Data note: The analysis is based on a representative sample of 4,886 records drawn from the full 126,832-record PubMed dataset. All percentages and rates are computed from this sample. Absolute counts cited in this report should be interpreted as proportional estimates, not exact totals from the full corpus. Temporal comparisons account for the natural PubMed indexing lag that concentrates older records in 2024 (≈80.3% of sample).

1

Publication Volume & Temporal Distribution

Analytical framing

  • The 2024 dominance (80.3% of sample: 3,924 records) reflects PubMed's real-world indexing lag — publications accumulate more indexed entries as time passes.
  • 2025 (737 records; 15.1%) and 2026 (225 records; 4.6%, Jan–Mar only) are structurally under-represented and should be benchmarked on rates, not raw counts.
  • Within 2024, 575 records (14.7%) have unknown publication month; 179 records in 2025 similarly lack month data. These are excluded from the monthly chart.

Fig 1a. Raw record counts by year in the 4,886-record sample. The strong 2024 skew is an indexing artifact, not evidence of declining research output.

Indexing lag effect: January 2024 alone accounts for 1,665 indexed records (42.5% of all 2024 month-known records) — likely because many late-2023 / early-2024 publications completed full indexing during this window.
2025 trajectory: Despite the smaller raw count, 2025 shows a consistent monthly baseline of ~30–94 indexed records. December 2025 (94 records) is the highest month of that year, suggesting end-of-year processing batch effects.
2026 early signal: March 2026 (98 records) already exceeds the 2025 monthly average (61.4), pointing to continued growth in biomedical research output.

Fig 1b. Month-by-month indexed publication counts. The dramatic January 2024 spike (1,665 records) reflects batch indexing of older records. Records with unknown publication month (575 in 2024; 179 in 2025) are excluded. 2026 data ends at March. Dashed vertical lines mark year boundaries.

Analytical caution: The steep 2024-to-2025 count decline is an artifact of indexing completeness, not a real-world decline in biomedical research activity. When comparing across years, normalize to monthly rates and use OA/type ratios rather than raw counts.
2

Geographic Landscape of Biomedical Research

Fig 2a. Top 10 contributing countries by total indexed publications (144 "Unknown" country records excluded). China and USA combined account for ~31% of the sample.

Fig 2b. Year-over-year country share (% of all indexed records). China's share dips in 2025 then recovers in early 2026. India's share rises notably in 2025 (3.3% → 8.0%), suggesting accelerating Indian research output or improved indexing coverage.

China's dominance: With 1,028 records (normalized), China contributes approximately 22.6% of 2024 publications, 13.2% in 2025, and 20.4% in 2026 — consistently the top single-nation contributor. The 2025 dip likely reflects indexing lag for Chinese-language journals that translates to PubMed later.
India's emergence: India's share nearly triples from 3.3% (2024) to 8.0% (2025), the largest proportional shift among major contributors. This warrants attention for funding strategists tracking research partnerships and citation networks.

3

Research Topic & MeSH Keyword Analysis

Coverage note: Only 52.9% of sample records have a major_topic assigned. Newer 2025–2026 publications are under-indexed due to MeSH indexing lag (MeSH assignment typically occurs weeks to months after initial PubMed indexing). Year-over-year topic comparisons should be treated as directional signals, not definitive volume counts.

Fig 3a. Top 20 major MeSH topics by total occurrence. COVID-19 remains the leading single topic (43 records), followed by Type 2 Diabetes and Breast Neoplasms.

Fig 3b. Top 15 substantive MeSH keywords (demographic/species terms excluded). Retrospective and cross-sectional study designs dominate, reflecting observational research norms. COVID-19 remains highly prevalent as a keyword even beyond its 2020–2022 peak.

Disease areas dominating: COVID-19, Type 2 Diabetes, Breast Neoplasms, and Alzheimer Disease head the major topic list — chronic disease burden and pandemic aftermath continue to drive research prioritization globally.
Microbiome on the rise: Gastrointestinal Microbiome ranks 4th overall with 16 records. Given that MeSH indexing lags for newer records, the actual volume of gut microbiome research is likely higher than this count suggests.
AI / digital health signal: Keywords such as "Algorithms" (47), "Signal Processing, Computer-Assisted" (26), and "Deep Learning" (appearing in major topics) indicate growing computational and AI-driven research, though raw counts remain modest in this sample.

4

Open Access Adoption & Journal Landscape

Fig 4a. Open access rate by publication year. 2025 records show the highest OA rate (74.1%), consistent with global policy trends toward mandated open access. The 2026 rate (53.8%) is lower, likely because recently indexed articles include more subscription-based journals not yet archived in PMC.

Fig 4b. Open access rates for the top 8 contributing countries. Iran leads at 86.9%, reflecting heavy reliance on open-access mega-journals. China's 55.7% rate is the lowest among major contributors — a strategic consideration for international citation visibility and policy alignment.

Fig 4c. Monthly open access rate trajectory (Jan 2024 – Mar 2026). Note high volatility in months with small sample sizes (e.g., Oct 2024: 42 records; Aug 2025: 26 records). The dashed reference line marks the 65% threshold. March 2026 shows a notable drop (23.5%) — this outlier likely reflects a batch of recently indexed subscription-journal articles not yet available via PMC.

Overall OA rate: 65.1% — nearly two-thirds of all indexed biomedical abstracts in this sample are accessible via PubMed Central. This is substantially above pre-2020 industry benchmarks (~40%) and reflects the impact of NIH, Wellcome Trust, and Plan S mandates.

Fig 4d. Top 10 journals by indexed volume. Scientific Reports (82), Heliyon (76), and Cureus (69) lead — all mega-journals with high OA rates and broad scope, reinforcing the OA publication trend. The IEEE EMBC conference proceedings (46) indicates significant biomedical engineering cross-over research.

5

Research Type Distribution & Collaboration Indicators

Fig 5a. Research type distribution across the full sample. Journal Articles dominate (84.5%). Reviews (8.3%), Case Reports (4.2%), Systematic Reviews (1.7%), and Preprints (0.8%) make up the remainder.

Fig 5b. Median author count by research type. Preprints have the highest median (9 authors), consistent with large collaborative bioRxiv submissions. Case Reports (5) and Reviews (5) reflect lower collaboration norms.

Preprint signal: Although preprints represent only 0.8% of records (41 articles), all are open access (100% OA rate) and have the highest median author count (9). This signals that high-collaboration, cutting-edge research is increasingly shared pre-publication.
Systematic Reviews: At only 1.7% of the sample (85 records) but with a 56.5% OA rate — the lowest among research types — there is a policy gap for mandating open access of high-impact synthesis publications.

6

Key Takeaways & Strategic Implications

Executive summary: The biomedical research landscape is shifting toward higher open-access publication, growing non-Western contributions (especially India), and continued dominance of chronic disease and pandemic-related topics. Early 2026 data suggests sustained output momentum.
01 Policy

Open Access Has Crossed a Structural Threshold

With 65.1% overall OA rate and 74.1% in 2025, open-access publication is now the majority norm in biomedical research. Funders should expect near-universal PMC compliance within 2–3 years. Plan S-aligned institutions should benchmark against the 74%+ level, not the old 40% baseline.

02 Trend

China & India Are the Key Non-Western Growth Stories

China holds a consistent ~20%+ share of indexed biomedical output. India's 2.4× share increase from 2024 to 2025 (3.3% → 8.0%) is the single most notable geographic shift. Strategists building international partnerships should prioritize both countries — particularly for clinical trial and epidemiological studies.

03 Trend

Chronic Disease & Microbiome Research Are the Core Growth Themes

Diabetes, cancer (breast, hepatocellular, lung, renal), neurodegenerative disease (Alzheimer, Parkinson), and gastrointestinal microbiome dominate the topic landscape. These remain the strongest candidates for sustained funding prioritization through 2027.

04 Policy

Systematic Reviews Face an Open Access Gap

Despite being the highest-impact research synthesis format, Systematic Reviews have the lowest OA rate in this sample (56.5%). This is below the 65.1% sample average and well below the Preprint (100%) and Case Report (80.8%) rates. Funders should consider targeted OA mandates for synthesis publications.

05 Trend

Preprints Signal a High-Collaboration Research Frontier

Preprints (all OA, median 9 authors) are the publication format with the highest collaboration intensity. As a leading indicator of incoming peer-reviewed output, monitoring preprint servers — especially bioRxiv — provides a 6–12 month forward view on emerging research priorities.

06 Data Risk

Indexing Lag Systematically Distorts Year-Over-Year Comparisons

The 2024 dominance (80.3% of sample) is a PubMed indexing artifact. Any internal report or dashboard comparing raw 2024 vs. 2025 counts without normalization will generate misleading conclusions about research output trajectory. Rate-based metrics (OA%, type%, country%) are the correct analytical currency.

07 Trend

Mega-Journals Now Dominate Biomedical Publishing Volume

Scientific Reports, Heliyon, and Cureus — all broad-scope, high-volume OA mega-journals — are the three most-indexed venues in this dataset. Their rise reflects a structural shift in where biomedical science is published, with implications for impact factor benchmarks and peer-review quality standards.

08 Policy

Early 2026 Data Confirms Continued Output Growth

March 2026 (98 records) already exceeds the 2025 monthly average (61.4 records/month). If this trajectory holds, 2026 will likely achieve comparable or greater output to 2025 once indexing catches up. Budget planning for 2027 funding cycles should assume continued expansion of indexed biomedical literature.

M

Methodology & Data Limitations

Dataset

  • Source: PubMed / NCBI via Kaggle (kanchana1990/biomedical-research-abstracts-20242026)
  • Full dataset: 126,832 records. Analytical sample used here: 4,886 records (representative subset).
  • Coverage: January 2024 – March 2026. All records are English-language.
  • QA applied: deduplication by PMID, abstract length filtering (50–1,000 words), date-range scoping.

Key Limitations

  • Temporal imbalance: ~80% of records are 2024 due to indexing lag. Year-over-year raw count comparisons are not meaningful; rates and proportions are used throughout.
  • MeSH coverage: Only 52.9% of records have a major_topic assigned. Emerging 2025–2026 topics are systematically under-represented.
  • Country normalization: "United States" and "USA" merged; "PR China" and "China" merged. 144 records with "Unknown" country are excluded from geographic analyses.
  • Open access definition: OA status reflects PMC availability at time of indexing — may not capture all OA pathways (e.g., institutional repositories, author manuscripts).
  • Sample size variability: Monthly OA rate calculations for small-count months (e.g., Oct 2024: 42 records) have high sampling variance.
